meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The only way to have a friend is to be one'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Emerson: it appears in his 1841 essay “Friendship,” where the popular version drops the first half of the sentence.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From Emerson’s essay “Friendship” ↗ in Essays: First Series (1841), where the full sentence reads “The only reward of virtue is virtue; the only way to have a friend is to be one.” This is one of the comparatively few famous Emerson lines that is correctly credited to him.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Near the essay’s close, paired with “The only reward of virtue is virtue”

source.excerpt: The only reward of virtue is virtue; the only way to have a friend is to be one.
trail: The complete sentence appears in the full text of Emerson’s “Friendship” ↗, first published in Essays: First Series (1841).
The Walden Woods Project ↗ lists it among its curated Emerson quotations, attributed to the essay “Friendship.”
Unlike many lines pinned on Emerson, this one is not flagged among the well-known Emerson misattributions ↗.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular version drops the first half of the sentence
source.excerptNote: Emerson sets the two clauses in parallel: friendship, like virtue, is not a prize you extract from others but something you become. Quoted alone, the second half loses that mirror.

author.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
author.heading: About Ralph Waldo Emerson
author.bio: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882) was the central figure of American Transcendentalism, a Boston-born essayist and lecturer whose Essays: First Series (1841) — including “Self-Reliance,” “Friendship,” and “Compensation” — shaped American thought about individualism and the moral life. His aphoristic style made him endlessly quotable, which is also why so many un-Emersonian lines now travel under his name; this one, however, is authentically his.
